## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Graffiti (`lumenary:graffiti`, a style that rests on this process)

_From: Philadelphia and New York streets, with stencil work from Paris; when: 1960s and 70s onward; works best on: High contrast portraits and bold silhouettes._

A stencil has no grey: a spot of the wall is either painted or it is not. That limit is what makes stencil portraits so striking, and this treatment keeps to it with three paint colours and a bare wall. The cut points come from the picture’s own brightness percentiles, so every photograph leaves about the same share of brick showing, however light or dark it is.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Paint a brick wall first, each brick slightly lighter or darker than its neighbours.
2. Find the 20th, 40th and 58th percentile brightness of this particular picture.
3. Use those points to cut three paint layers and a bare area, like a multi-layer stencil.
4. Add a blurred copy of the stencil at low strength as overspray, plus a fine scatter of dots.
5. Start a drip wherever paint sits directly above bare wall, then outline and fill the tag.

**The maths:**

$$\text{level}=\begin{cases}3&L<q_{0.20}\\2&L<q_{0.40}\\1&L<q_{0.58}\\0&\text{otherwise (bare wall)}\end{cases}$$

_q is a quantile of the picture’s brightness values._ (primitives: tone-bands)

$$C=(1-\alpha)\,C_{\text{sharp}}+\alpha\,C_{\text{blur}},\qquad \alpha=0.35\cdot\text{overspray}$$

_Overspray: the blurred copy is blended over the sharp one._ (primitives: mix-over, blur)

**Dials:** `palette` (Cans) = "street" (street, toxic, ocean); `wall` (Wall) = "brick" (brick, grey, plaster); `spray` (Overspray) = 55 [0 to 100]; `drips` (Drips) = 45 [0 to 100]; `tag` (Tag) = "LUMEN"; `seed` (Respray) = 1.

**History:** Modern graffiti took shape in Philadelphia in the late 1960s and in New York in the 1970s, where tags such as TAKI 183 were noticed by the press in 1971. Stencil work followed, with artists such as Blek le Rat in Paris in the early 1980s and later Banksy, who used the speed of a cut stencil to put detailed images on walls in seconds.
